structural synaptic changes are present in the substantia gellatinosa of the spinal cord months after complete peripheral nerve injury, and that these changes are likely to contribute to the maintenance of neuropathic pains.
the substantia gelatniosa in the spinal cord is a target for structural changes following peripheral nerve injury and that these structural changes may contribute to neuropathic allodynia.
structural changes in the central nervous system may contribute to maintaining chronic pain states.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of neuropathic (nerve injury-induced) pain, which is a frequent and severe complication after nerve injuries.
the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying chronic neuropathic and inflammatory pain states.
the mechanisms underlying the transition from acute to chronic pain, and with the development of new treatment strategies for neuropathic pain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present study provides a novel model of chronic neuropathy and that the model can be used to study the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying chronic neuropathic conditions.
the structural synaptic changes observed in the substantia-gelatinosa in a complete sciatic nerve injury model, may be involved in the maintenance of neuropathic allodynia.
the synaptic changes we observed are not sufficient to cause neuropathic pain by themselves but may be part of a network of changes that contribute to the maintenance of CNP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
structural synaptic changes in the spinal cord can be induced by chronic nerve injury, but are not necessarily required for the maintenance of neuropathic hyperalgesia.
the synaptic plasticity in the dorsal horn is a long-lasting process and is likely to contribute to the persistence of neuropathic symptoms.
the structural synaptic plasticity in the dorsal horn is a key component in maintaining chronic neuropathic states.
The main takeaway from our work is that
structural changes in central pain processing circuits can be detected months after complete nerve sectioning.
structural changes in the central nervous system are not only important in the onset of neuropathy, but also in the maintenance of chronic neuropathics states.
